## My request:
it is the industry standard for versioning and collaborating on code. However, we envision it as a tool that is suitable for local-first knowledge work as well, which is why we built `sun` as a git extension, and envision it for use cases beyond coding. git was originally appealing due to it being a very effective, local first tool for versioning. While it's very different from version history systems you'd see in general knowledge work platforms like Google Docs and Notion, there are concepts from git that you'd want in a knowledge work system. Commits act as your historical log, and branches and PRs act as "drafts". Similar to being able to revert to a point in time in version history, you can also revert commits to reach a particular state. Fundamentally, the experience of git is much more bearing of agent workload. It's easy to review PRs, and see them as separate units of work and focus. You can review two PRs that edit one code file, and understand the change that you're merging very clearly. Compare this to suggest mode from popular document editors. They're unable to support many agents working on many overlapping documents at once.\
 Here are some of the problems they'll run into: 

1. All suggested edits are applied to "live state". This is the current, most up-to-date version of the document. It means that whenever a change is made (even if it was made after the suggestions), the suggestions will render on top of this live state. There is no way to branch off of a particular point in history, so suggestions may be outdated or confusing. With git, you don't have this problem because you have branches and merge conflicts.
2. If many agents make suggestions on a page at once, you'll see them all at the same time, meaning there's a lot of bottleneck for manual review.
3. Typically, suggestions on popular document editors are independent. However, when an agent makes suggestions, usually the suggestions are grouped by a turn. Suggestions make more logical sense when you can see their grouping. And when they're rejected or accepted, we should get signal on the agents actions during that turn.

Git is the industry standard for versioning and collaborating on code. We built `sun` as a Git extension because we see its local-first model as a strong foundation for knowledge work, too.

Commits preserve a history of changes. Branches provide independent drafts, and pull requests package those changes for review. Earlier states remain recoverable, and conflicting edits can be resolved explicitly.

These concepts become especially useful when multiple agents work on overlapping documents. Reviewers can assess each proposal as a coherent unit, even when several proposals touch the same file. Document editors’ suggestion modes make this harder:

1. **Suggestions sit on a changing document.** As the document evolves, their original context can become unclear. Branches preserve a proposal’s starting point and make conflicts explicit.
2. **Suggestions compete for attention.** Edits from multiple agents appear together, creating a crowded review surface. Pull requests separate them into focused proposals.
3. **Suggestions lose their grouping.** An agent’s related edits often express one intent. Reviewing them together makes that intent clearer and provides more meaningful feedback when the proposal is accepted or rejected.

The opportunity is to bring Git’s coherent units of work and review to knowledge work, without requiring users to manage every individual edit.
